title: WebRL Breakdown: How the ICLR 2025 Paper Frames Self-Evolving Curriculum as a Closed Loop
subtitle: Reading a Web Agent Reinforcement Learning Paper from the Perspective of Structural Anatomy
markdown: > Breakdown Target: WebRL: Training LLM Web Agents via Self-Evolving Online Curriculum Reinforcement Learning, ICLR 2025. Authors from Tsinghua University and Zhipu AI; open-source code is available at THUDM/WebRL. Similar to the previous breakdown of Search-R1, here we only analyze why the structure is effective. All numbers are from the latest arXiv version of the paper and can be cross-checked against the original tables. ## I. Problem Definition: A One-Shot Statement of Three Dilemmas When using open-source models as web agents, the Introduction explicitly names three dilemmas: 1. **Task Scarcity**: Environments like WebArena-Lite have limited training tasks, and static data is quickly exhausted. 2. **Sparse Feedback**: There are only terminal success/failure signals for tasks, with no step-by-step rewards. 3. **Distribution Shift**: Online learning and curriculum progression cause policy instability, where newly acquired abilities overwrite old ones. The Methods section subsequently addresses these three issues one by one with corresponding components, mapping challenges to components. This is the structural skeleton most worth learning from this paper. ## II. Structural Unconventionality: Related Works Placed in Section 4 The common layout for NLP conference papers places Related Works immediately after the Introduction; WebRL places it after the experiments and before the conclusion. The benefit is immediately visible: the end of the Introduction is directly followed by the method overview diagram (Figure 2), allowing readers to go from 'pain points' to 'solutions' with zero distance. The first read does not require traversing ten citations first. ML conferences have a high acceptance rate for this layout, and authors can actively leverage this convention difference when submitting. ## III. Mapping of Three Challenges to Three Components | Challenge | Component | Structural Location | Exclusive Validation | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Task Scarcity | Self-evolving Curriculum: Failure Task Generator + Critic Difficulty Filtering | 2.1 | 3.9 Case Analysis | | Sparse Feedback | ORM (Outcome-Supervised Reward Model) | 2 Main Text | 3.8 Standalone ORM Evaluation | | Distribution Shift | KL Constraint + Experience Replay + Perplexity Filtering | 2.2 | 3.7 Ablation | Each component has a dedicated subsection in the experiment section for independent testing, with methods and experiments being completely symmetric. The modular structure, allowing components to be independently assembled or disassembled, enables reviewers to verify contributions item by item and facilitates subsequent work citing individual components separately. Key designs of the three components: 1. **Self-evolving Curriculum**: Uses previously failed instructions as seeds for in-breadth expansion to generate new tasks; the critic scores based on initial states, retaining only instructions in the 0.05 to 0.75 range to ensure task feasibility and difficulty matching current capabilities; GPT-4o is then used to automatically exclude tasks that are fundamentally impossible to complete in the environment. 2. **ORM**: A large language model (LLM) reward model that provides a binary decision by comparing the probabilities of outputting YES versus NO. The input consists of the instruction, historical actions, and final state HTML. The test set accuracy is 80.8%, higher than GPT-4's 71.9% and GPT-4V's 71.2%. 3. **Policy Update**: Maximum entropy RL objective with KL constraint and entropy regularization; off-policy loss L = E[(β log(πθ/πref) − A*)²]; experience replay stores only successful trajectories, filtered by the previous stage actor's perplexity. The optimal action interval is [1/0.95, 1/0.5] (average success rate 31.5% in this interval, compared to 29.1% and 23.0% in the side intervals respectively). ## Section IV: Analysis Chain in the Experiment Section: From Main Results to Single-Component Validation The 9 subsections in the experiment section form a three-layer progressive chain: | Level | Section | Role | | --- | --- | --- | | Overall Effectiveness | 3.1 Environment and Baselines, 3.2 Main Results, 3.3 Scale Effects | WebArena-Lite comprises 165 test cases; all three base models significantly outperform the baseline | | Mechanism Explanation | 3.4 Error Type Distribution, 3.5 Step Count Stratification, 3.6 Complexity Stratification | Explains "why it works": significantly reduces mid-process stuck loops; tasks with long steps and high complexity show the greatest advantages | | Component Verification | 3.7 Ablation, 3.8 ORM Evaluation, 3.9 Case Studies | Isolates and individually verifies each component | The four ablation variants are designed cleanly: removing the replay buffer, removing the KL constraint, removing both, and removing curriculum learning; each time only one component is altered. The conclusions hold independently: without the buffer, performance deteriorates over time; the KL constraint consistently outperforms REINFORCE-style updates; and removing curriculum learning results in a lower upper bound. ## V. Opening Figure Directly Establishes the Argument Figure 1 is placed in the Introduction: a comparison of success rates between proprietary and open-source models. GLM-4 and Llama after WebRL training stand on the far right, while GPT-4-Turbo's 17.6% is suppressed below. All key numbers from the abstract are condensed into this figure: | Model | WebArena-Lite Success Rate | | --- | --- | | Llama-3.1-8B (Pre-training → Post-training) | 4.8% → 42.4% | | GLM-4-9B (Pre-training → Post-training) | 6.1% → 43.0% | | Llama-3.1-70B (Pre-training → Post-training) | 12.7% → 49.1% | | Same Base 8B using SFT | 20.6% | | GPT-4-Turbo / GPT-4o | 17.6% / 13.9% | | Previously open-source best AutoWebGLM | 18.2% | This represents a relative improvement of over 160% compared to GPT-4-Turbo. Readers scanning the figure can immediately grasp the claim; such 'conclusion-first' figures are worth prioritizing in design. ## 6. Three Techniques for Learning to Walk 1. **Mapping of Challenge, Component, and Verification**: Each subsection in the Method section has a corresponding dual subsection in the Experiment section, allowing reviewers to verify contributions without having to piece things together themselves. 2. **Ablation designed as independent, detachable variants**: Each variant removes only one component, so any single conclusion can be cited independently. 3. **Three-part structure in the appendix to demonstrate the legitimacy of the method**: Appendix A sequentially provides derivations (A.1), theoretical proofs (A.2), and a comparison table of characteristics with DPO/PPO/AWR (A.3 Table 4), pushing the complete argument for 'why this update rule holds' to the appendix, keeping the main text lightweight. ## Postscript: Mapping to My Own Work The essence of the self-evolution course is growing training tasks from failure: failed instructions serve as seeds, the critic constrains the difficulty range, and task difficulty extrapolates with capability. During the Phase 0 data feasibility verification for the QQ Speed post-race coach, this approach offers direct reference value: in scenarios with insufficient cold-start data, the 'generation and filtering' pipeline of tasks itself can become part of data construction, allowing the training set to grow alongside the model's capabilities. ## References - Paper: arXiv:2411.02337, published at ICLR 2025 (Poster) - Code: github.com/THUDM/WebRL - OpenReview：forum?id=oVKEAFjEqv
